## Introduction

This article shows where time and memory go in a cuplyr pipeline, when to use
eager or lazy execution, and where the GPU loses to plain dplyr. The numbers
come from one machine. `vignette("query-optimization", package = "cuplyr")`
explains the optimizer passes. This article measures what they buy.

In short, use lazy (the default) for pipelines. It is not faster. On clean GPU
memory it ties with eager up to 1e6 rows and is 0.67 to 1.0 ms slower at 1e7
and 5e7 rows. Its advantage is memory. Lazy frees every intermediate column when the
pipeline finishes. Eager keeps them until R's garbage collector runs, so in a
loop they pile up until the card is full and cuplyr's out-of-memory handler has
to step in. In the measurements below that made eager 3 to 7 times slower than
lazy.

```{r setup}
library(cuplyr)
library(dplyr)
```

## How a cuplyr call runs

Each verb does some work in R, such as checking arguments and working out the
new schema. In eager mode it then runs on the GPU. At 1e3 rows the R part
dominates. A profile of one eager verb at 1e3 rows put about 80% of the time in
R for `filter()`, `mutate()` and `arrange()`, 98% for `select()` and 61 to 65%
for a grouped `summarise()`. That fixed cost is the per-call floor.

The two modes differ in when the GPU work happens.

- Eager runs each verb at once and returns a GPU table. Every intermediate
  table stays allocated until R's garbage collector drops it.
- Lazy records each verb as a node in a plan without touching the GPU.
  `compute()` optimizes and runs the plan and keeps the result on the GPU.
  `collect()` does the same and copies the result to R. Intermediates are freed
  when the call returns.

To use eager, pass `tbl_gpu(df, lazy = FALSE)` for one table, or set
`options(cuplyr.exec_mode = "eager")` or `CUPLYR_EXEC_MODE=eager` for every
table created afterwards (see `?"cuplyr-options"`). Printing a lazy table runs
the plan to show its first rows and keeps nothing, so it costs about as much as
a `collect()`.

`show_query()` prints the pending steps of a lazy table. `explain()` also
prints the plan the optimizer will run.

```{r explain, eval = FALSE}
lazy <- tbl_gpu(mtcars) |>
  filter(mpg > 20) |>
  mutate(kpl = mpg * 0.425, hp2 = hp * 2) |>
  select(cyl, kpl)

explain(lazy)
#> Pending operations:
#> ast_select [2 cols]
#> | ast_mutate [2 expressions]
#> | | ast_filter [1 predicates]
#> | | | ast_source [11 cols]
#>
#> AST depth: 4
#> Node count: 4
#>
#> Optimized plan:
#> ast_select [2 cols]
#> | ast_mutate [1 expressions]
#> | | ast_filter [1 predicates]
#> | | | ast_select [2 cols]
#> | | | | ast_source [11 cols]
```

```{r explain-run, echo = FALSE}
# The output above is pasted so a default build shows it. A build with GPU
# evaluation runs the same code and fails if explain() no longer prints it.
lazy <- tbl_gpu(mtcars) |>
  filter(mpg > 20) |>
  mutate(kpl = mpg * 0.425, hp2 = hp * 2) |>
  select(cyl, kpl)
stopifnot(identical(
  trimws(capture.output(explain(lazy))),
  c("Pending operations:",
    "ast_select [2 cols]",
    "| ast_mutate [2 expressions]",
    "| | ast_filter [1 predicates]",
    "| | | ast_source [11 cols]",
    "",
    "AST depth: 4",
    "Node count: 4",
    "",
    "Optimized plan:",
    "ast_select [2 cols]",
    "| ast_mutate [1 expressions]",
    "| | ast_filter [1 predicates]",
    "| | | ast_select [2 cols]",
    "| | | | ast_source [11 cols]")
))
```

In the optimized plan the mutate has one expression instead of two, because
nothing uses `hp2`. A new select right above the source keeps only the 2
columns the filter and the mutate read. Nothing has run on the GPU yet. `collect(lazy)` runs the plan.

`compute()` and `collect()` run six optimizer passes.

- Projection pruning adds a select that keeps only the columns later steps
  need. This is the inner select above.
- Mutate fusion merges consecutive `mutate()` calls into one step, keeping the
  order you wrote. It skips the merge if the result would have more than 8
  expressions, or if the later `mutate()` reads more than 4 columns the earlier
  one creates.
- Dead-column pruning drops mutate outputs nothing uses, like `hp2` above.
- Filter pushdown moves a filter below a mutate when the filter doesn't read a
  column the mutate computes, so the mutate sees fewer rows. It also moves
  filters below a `select()` that keeps their columns, and into the inputs of
  some joins. That depends on the join type and its `relationship`, `multiple`
  and `unmatched` arguments. `explain()` shows where each filter ended up.
- Filter reordering merges consecutive `filter()` calls into one node that
  builds one row mask, and puts cheaper predicates first, judged by expression
  size. Eager runs each `filter()` separately and allocates a table between
  them.
- Scan pushdown hands filters on a lazy `read_parquet_gpu()` table to the
  parquet reader, so it skips data it doesn't need to read.

A single `filter()` with several predicates is already one node in both modes,
and the optimizer leaves its predicate order alone unless it merges it with
another filter. Verbs such as `arrange()` and `summarise()` are barriers. The
passes run on each side of them but not across.

## Measurements

The tables below are static. Nothing is timed when this vignette builds. The
code is at the end.

- Date and version: 2026-10-26, cuplyr 0.1.1.9000, at the version from the NEWS
  entry "Faster eager verb calls". Some figures from earlier versions are quoted
  for comparison.
- Hardware and software: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 (12 GB), driver 615.78.08,
  R 4.6.1, dplyr 1.2.1, the default `async` memory resource.
- Method: data already on the GPU, so uploads are not in the pipeline timings.
  Warm runs, median of 15 samples (9 at 5e7 rows). Each sample times a batch of
  calls fenced with `gpu_sync()`, aiming at 30 ms per batch. Calls slower than
  30 ms ran one per batch. `gc()` ran untimed before every batch. Each number is
  the median of three fresh R processes, which differed by up to 4% for the
  cuplyr pipelines and up to 10% elsewhere. The timer has 1 ms resolution, so
  gaps of 0.1 ms between eager and lazy at 1e3 and 1e6 rows are noise.
- Some figures under "Reading the results" come from separate profiling runs.
  The text says where.

### A five-verb pipeline

```r
filter(x > 0.1) |> mutate(z = x * y + w) |> group_by(g) |>
  summarise(m = mean(z), n = n()) |> arrange(desc(m)) |> collect()
```

The table has an integer `g` with 100 groups and double columns `x`, `y` and
`w`. The dplyr column runs the same pipeline on a tibble. "Held" is the GPU
memory one call leaves allocated until R's next `gc()`, measured as the growth
of `gpu_memory_state()$pool_used_bytes`.

| rows | eager ms | lazy ms | dplyr ms | eager held MB | lazy held MB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1e3 | 1.87 | 1.75 | 3.50 | 0.04 | 0 |
| 1e6 | 2.00 | 2.00 | 22.0 | 32 | 0 |
| 1e7 | 4.33 | 5.00 | 213 | 324 | 0 |
| 5e7 | 17.5 | 18.5 | not run | 1620 | 0 |
| 5e7, 5 calls back to back, no `gc()` | 68.4 | 18.0 | not run | | |

The last row is what a loop does. It runs the pipeline five times without a
`gc()` and reports the mean time per call. The eager figure depends on what the
memory pool already holds, and 68.4 ms is the low end. In two earlier runs of
the same loop (commit b39a8f1) eager took 145 and 155 ms per call, against 22
and 24 ms for lazy.

### One eager verb at 1e3 rows

No `collect()`. The result stays on the GPU.

| verb | cuplyr ms | dplyr ms |
|---|---|---|
| filter | 0.36 | 0.35 |
| mutate | 0.37 | 0.39 |
| select | 0.10 | 0.42 |
| arrange | 0.14 | 0.68 |
| grouped summarise | 0.40 | 0.77 |

### Transfers (4 columns)

| rows | `tbl_gpu()` upload ms | `collect()` of all rows ms |
|---|---|---|
| 1e3 | 0.13 | 0.10 |
| 1e6 | 6.00 | 6.00 |
| 1e7 | 63.0 | 54.0 |

### A case built for the optimizer

A 21-column table (`g` plus `x1` to `x20`) and a query that computes columns it
later drops and filters after the mutate:

```r
mutate(a = x1 * 2, b = x2 * x3, c = x4 + x5) |> filter(x1 > 0.9) |>
  select(g, a) |> collect()
```

`explain()` shows the optimizer reading 2 of the 21 columns, moving the filter
below the mutate, and dropping `b` and `c`.

| rows | eager ms | lazy ms | dplyr ms | eager held MB | lazy held MB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1e6 | 1.73 | 1.73 | 22.5 | 43 | 0 |
| 1e7 | 6.20 | 4.86 | 183 | 428 | 0 |

### Reading the results

- Up to 1e6 rows lazy ties with eager or is a little faster. With longer
  batches (0.15 s each, 11 interleaved samples, three fresh processes) lazy took
  1.75 to 1.76 ms against 1.87 to 1.88 at 1e3 rows, and 1.95 to 1.98 ms against
  2.05 to 2.08 at 1e6, 4 to 6% less. At 1e7 rows lazy is 0.67 ms behind (5.00
  against 4.33 ms, 15%) and at 5e7 rows 1.0 ms behind (18.5 against 17.5 ms,
  6%). Before the NEWS entry "Faster lazy verb calls" those two gaps were 1.2
  and 1.5 ms.
- At 1e3 rows, in two profiling runs, recording the five-verb lazy plan took
  1.0 ms, all of it in R. `collect()` took 0.66 ms: 0.04 ms to optimize, 0.43 ms
  to lower and run, 0.09 ms to copy the result to R, and the rest bookkeeping.
  Recording time doesn't depend on row count.
- Lazy is slower on big tables because it loses overlap. At 1e7 rows, in a
  profiling run, `collect()` took 3.8 ms, 3.6 ms of it lowering and running the
  plan. The optimizer leaves this plan unchanged, so both modes run the same
  five GPU steps. An eager verb returns while its GPU work is still running, so
  the next verb's R work runs alongside it. Lazy does all its R work first while
  the GPU waits. Forcing eager to wait after every verb removes the overlap. In
  three runs eager took 4.25 to 4.33 ms normally, 5.14 to 5.17 ms with a
  `gpu_sync()` after each verb, and lazy took 5.00 ms. So lost overlap accounts
  for all of lazy's 0.67 ms. The overlap grows with the GPU work, which is why
  the gap shows only on big tables. Freeing lazy's intermediates adds about
  0.05 ms at every size.
- In the optimizer case lazy wins only on the bigger table, 4.86 against
  6.20 ms at 1e7 rows (22% less). At 1e6 rows both take 1.73 ms because there is
  too little GPU work for the skipped steps to matter.
- Adding a `filter()` or `mutate()` to a lazy plan took 0.16 to 0.19 ms at every
  plan length from 1 to 100 verbs, in a profiling run. `collect()` time grows
  with plan length. A 100-verb plan of `mutate()` calls took 8.8 ms. Joins are
  the exception. Recording one on a 120-node plan took about twice as long as on
  a 3-node plan (0.61 against 0.30 ms).
- Memory is the reason to prefer lazy. The eager pipeline leaves about 32 bytes
  per row behind until R's next `gc()`, 324 MB at 1e7 rows and 1620 MB at 5e7.
  Run it again before the `gc()` and the pool keeps growing. In a traced run of
  the five-call loop it went from 5.4 to 11.6 GB on a 12 GB card. Then cuplyr's
  out-of-memory handler ran `gc()` and `gpu_gc()` and retried the step. That is
  the back-to-back row, 68.4 against 18.0 ms, lazy 3.8 times faster. The two
  earlier runs gave 6.6 and 6.7 times.
- Until the card fills, eager stays faster. In a separate run at 2.5e7 rows,
  five back-to-back eager calls left about 4 GB behind and took 9.2 ms each,
  against 10 ms lazy.
- Against dplyr at 1e3 rows both modes are about twice as fast (1.87 ms eager
  and 1.75 ms lazy against 3.50 ms). At 1e6 rows cuplyr is 11 times faster, and
  at 1e7 rows 43 to 49 times.

## Where the GPU loses

- Tiny tables. At 1e3 rows `filter()` and `mutate()` take as long as dplyr's
  (0.36 and 0.37 ms against 0.35 and 0.39), because R-side work dominates.
  `select()`, `arrange()` and grouped `summarise()` are 4.2, 4.8 and 1.9 times
  faster. A whole pipeline is about twice as fast, but that saves under 2 ms.
- Transfers. Moving data costs more than computing on it. Uploading 1e7 rows
  takes 63 ms and collecting them 54 ms, against 4.33 ms for the eager pipeline.
  If you upload, run one cheap verb and collect, the GPU loses.
- CPU fallbacks. Some expressions have no GPU translation, so cuplyr evaluates
  them in R and copies data across. This is silent by default. Set
  `options(cuplyr.fallback = "warn")` to be told, or `"error"` to forbid it. The
  message names the verb, the expression, the reason and how much data was
  copied. A plan break is different. It happens when a lazy plan has to run
  early, for example a `summarise()` of an integer `sum(i + j)`, and it stays on
  the GPU. `options(cuplyr.plan_break = "warn")` reports it, and it never errors.
  See `?"cuplyr-fallback"`.

## Practical advice

- Upload once, keep the data on the GPU, and collect once at the end.
- Use lazy for pipelines, especially on big tables and in loops. Don't expect it
  to be faster. Its gain is that intermediates don't pile up.
- Use eager for interactive exploration and single calls where you want each
  result at once.
- To branch from a shared prefix, `compute()` it once and build the branches
  from the result, which stays on the GPU.
- After dropping a large eager result, `gc()` returns its memory to cuplyr's
  pool for the next calls to reuse. `gpu_gc()` also hands the pool's unused
  memory back to the card for other processes. It takes about a second and the
  pool has to grow again afterwards, so don't call it inside a loop. See
  `vignette("memory", package = "cuplyr")`.
- Fence GPU timings with `gpu_sync()`. GPU calls return before the kernels
  finish, so without it the timer can stop early.
- Check `explain()` when a lazy pipeline is slower than you expect.

## Reproduce

This is a trimmed copy of the script behind the pipeline timings and the memory
column. It doesn't run when the vignette builds. Run it in a fresh session on an
idle GPU. Batch sizes come from one timed call that the 1 ms timer rounds, so
batches of sub-millisecond calls can run well under or over the 30 ms target.

```{r reproduce, eval = FALSE}
library(cuplyr)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1)

# Median ms per call. A sample is a batch of calls fenced with gpu_sync();
# gc() runs untimed before every batch.
per_call <- function(fn, samples = 15, warmup = 3, target = 0.03) {
  for (i in seq_len(warmup)) fn()
  gpu_sync(); gc(verbose = FALSE)
  t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]; fn(); gpu_sync()
  one <- max(proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0, 1e-4)
  reps <- max(1L, min(500L, as.integer(ceiling(target / one))))
  t <- vapply(seq_len(samples), function(i) {
    gc(verbose = FALSE)
    t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
    for (j in seq_len(reps)) fn()
    gpu_sync()
    (proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0) / reps
  }, numeric(1))
  1e3 * median(t)
}

# GPU memory one call leaves allocated until R's next gc(), in MB.
held_mb <- function(fn) {
  gc(verbose = FALSE); gc(verbose = FALSE); gpu_sync()
  u0 <- gpu_memory_state()$pool_used_bytes
  r <- fn(); gpu_sync()
  u1 <- gpu_memory_state()$pool_used_bytes
  rm(r)
  (u1 - u0) / 1e6
}

pipeline <- function(d) {
  d |>
    filter(x > 0.1) |>
    mutate(z = x * y + w) |>
    group_by(g) |>
    summarise(m = mean(z), n = n()) |>
    arrange(desc(m))
}

n <- 1e6
df <- data.frame(g = sample.int(100L, n, TRUE), x = runif(n), y = runif(n),
                 w = rnorm(n))
tb <- tibble::as_tibble(df)
eg <- tbl_gpu(df, lazy = FALSE)
lz <- tbl_gpu(df, lazy = TRUE)

c(eager = per_call(function() collect(pipeline(eg))),
  lazy  = per_call(function() collect(pipeline(lz))),
  dplyr = per_call(function() pipeline(tb)))
c(eager = held_mb(function() collect(pipeline(eg))),
  lazy  = held_mb(function() collect(pipeline(lz))))
```
